concept: Crypto trading strategies with evidence: basis carry, funding arbitrage, delta-neutral, and what survives costs
summary: Evidence status: research claims ungated (v4 evidence gate not passed); treat as leads with cited sources. Educational reference, not financial advice. The pack catalogues cited research units on crypto strategies (basis carry, funding arbitrage, delta-neutral, and what survives costs): perpetual-versus-spot basis capture (cash and carry) and funding-rate arbitrage including Ethena USDe, grid trading and market making, momentum versus mean reversion, and backtest overfitting (Probability of Backtest Overfitting, deflated Sharpe), with fees and slippage threaded through each; disagreements sit under Contested.

facts.text: Funding is not synchronized across venues, so some practitioners trade perp against perp with no spot leg: long where funding is negative, short where it is neutral or positive. askrubyai lists the costs: margin on two venues, different settlement timing (Binance every 8 hours, Hyperliquid hourly) and one leg liquidating before the other. It reports no PnL for the idea.

The Probability of Backtest Overfitting (PBO) is the probability that the configuration chosen as best in-sample ranks below the median of all N configurations out-of-sample. Bailey, Borwein, Lopez de Prado and Zhu estimate it with combinatorially symmetric cross-validation (CSCV): split the matrix of per-configuration returns into S time blocks, form every half/half train-test combination, and record the out-of-sample rank of the in-sample winner. It needs the return series of every trial. They call the method model-free and non-parametric and say standard hold-out techniques are unreliable a

A grid bot is a range/mean-reversion bet: it earns small gains while price oscillates and gives most of them back in trending stretches. A preprint shows that under simple assumptions, without any view on trend, a traditional grid has essentially zero expected return. A six-month Gate.io BTC-perp practitioner log reports 'small gains in ranging months' returned in trends, net roughly flat to modest after fees, with no buy-and-hold comparison.

Headline gross returns from crypto signal studies are not evidence of tradable edge: both independent tests found the reversal signal profitable before costs and unprofitable after realistic fees given high turnover, so any citation of a gross Sharpe or gross return without a cost model should be discounted.

Cross-exchange arbitrage is an example of an edge that stopped paying. Makarov and Schoar document large, recurrent price deviations across exchanges, much larger across countries than within them, and link them to capital controls on arbitrage capital. Crepelliere, Pelster and Zeisberger (Journal of Financial Markets, 2023) find that the magnitude of arbitrage opportunities decreased greatly from April 2018 and that exploiting existing price differences has been barely possible since. Neither abstract discusses fees.

The same paper's Dynamic Grid Trading (DGT) strategy resets the grid around the current price whenever price breaks the range. Its backtests use Binance spot 1-minute data for BTC and ETH (January 2021 to July 2024), a 0.08% maker fee that the paper describes as OKX Level 1, and at most one grid transaction per minute. It models no slippage or leverage, has no out-of-sample split, reports no Sharpe ratio and gives no per-asset result table. The text reports DGT IRR as high as 60-70%. Binance and Hyperliquid compute funding as the premium index plus clamp(interest rate - premium index, -0.05%, +0.05%), with the interest component fixed at 0.01% per 8 hours (Binance: 0.03% per day; Hyperliquid: 0.00125% per hour, quoted as 11.6% APR paid to shorts). Positive funding means longs pay shorts, and only positions open at the settlement time pay or receive: Binance settles at 00:00, 08:00 and 16:00 UTC, while Hyperliquid accrues hourly at one-eighth of the 8-hour rate on oracle-price notional. He et al. confirm the Binance clamp (gamma = 0.05%) and say Hyperliquid mirrors it.

Because of the clamp, funding equals the 0.01% interest component whenever the premium index lies between -0.04% and +0.06% (derived from the formula), so a short collects a positive baseline of about 10.95% a year (simple) when perp and spot sit close together. Empirically, He et al. (sample 2020-01 to 2024-03) find the premium inside the clamp region in about 36-45% of hours and 42-50% of Binance settlements paid exactly the interest component; a BitMEX press release says funding was positive in over 92% of Q3 2025 across BitMEX, Binance and Hyperliquid, even when perps traded at a slight di

The standard funding formula adds a fixed interest component of 0.01% per 8 hours (about 11% a year) paid to shorts, so funding sits at that baseline whenever the perp trades near spot. BitMEX measured funding positive for more than 92% of Q3 2025 across BitMEX, Binance and Hyperliquid, and exactly 0.01% for 78.19% (BTC) and 87.52% (ETH) of the quarter on BitMEX. Cadence differs by venue: Binance settles every 8 hours (TIA every 4 hours), while Hyperliquid pays every hour at one-eighth of the computed 8-hour rate and caps funding at 0.5% per hour.

Part of the conflict in the cross-sectional momentum literature likely comes from formation horizon and coin universe, not from whether momentum exists. Grobys and Sapkota used monthly returns and 2 to 12 month windows (as Grobys et al. 2025 summarise them), which sit past the one-month turn Dobrynskaya reports. The HSE write-up of Dobrynskaya's study says results differ because studies use different, often small, coin samples, periods and holding durations. The published DSR formula adjusts for sample length, skewness and kurtosis but has no autocorrelation term. Quantt says autocorrelation and fat tails widen the sampling distribution of SR, so its i.i.d. Gaussian noise tables are optimistic (real noise produces bigger flukes), and it points to Lo (2002) for the autocorrelation correction. The open-source backtest-audit repo adds a Newey-West lag-1 autocorrelation correction to its DSR; that is an add-on, not part of the 2014 paper, and the repo code was not audited here.

With separate spot and perp accounts each leg must be capitalised against its own liquidation; He et al.'s event study finds perp-spot deviations compressed significantly after Binance introduced portfolio margining on 20 Apr 2022, which nets the legs inside one account and so raised arbitrage capacity. Funding-rate arbitrage holds spot (or a staked asset) long against an equal short perpetual and earns the funding that longs pay shorts when the perp trades above spot. Funding is a peer-to-peer transfer between traders (Hyperliquid's docs: no fee is collected on it). Ethena's USDe runs this trade at scale: its short BTC/ETH perps sit on centralized exchanges while the backing assets stay with off-exchange settlement providers such as Copper, Ceffu and Fireblocks. sUSDe yield comes from funding, staking yield on LST collateral, short-dated futures basis and interest on liquid stablecoins, and

USDe's backing is hedged by short BTC/ETH perpetual futures on centralized exchanges, and yield to stakers comes from funding on those shorts, staking yield on LST collateral, short-dated futures basis, and interest on liquid stablecoin/Treasury-like holdings; the mix shifts toward stables when funding falls below Treasury yields.

Reported Sharpe ratios for the carry trade depend on how the author samples and marks the legs. BIS notes that a trade held to expiry has a known payoff, which gives an 'infinite Sharpe ratio problem', so it reports each leg separately and an equal-weighted monthly combination (Sharpe about 0.6). CMU computes 8-hour excess returns for a long-spot, short-perpetual position on Binance and annualizes with 1,095 periods a year (Table 3 Sharpe: 11.5 USDT-margined, 6.4 coin-margined). CMU's cash-flow tables state that they abstract from transaction costs and margin requirements.

Ethena sizes its perp hedge by carry and by open interest, not by supply. LlamaRisk (10 Oct 2025) describes the rule: the perp share grows only if funding exceeds the base rate (T-bill or Aave stablecoin supply rate) and open interest can absorb more short interest. When supply reached about $14.6B, open interest did not grow enough, so Ethena parked inflows in Aave stablecoin markets (peak aUSDT $1.63B, aUSDC $1.32B). What overfitting does out-of-sample depends on memory. For a memoryless random walk, selecting the best in-sample configuration leaves expected out-of-sample performance at the process mean (zero if there is no skill). If the performance series has compensation effects, such as a global constraint or first-order serial correlation (the authors use AR(1) with phi = 0.995, half-life 138 observations), higher in-sample SR implies lower out-of-sample SR (their Proposition 6.3) and the IS/OOS regression slope is significantly negative. The Deflated Sharpe Ratio (Bailey and López de Prado, Journal of Portfolio Management 40(5), 2014) corrects an observed Sharpe ratio for selection bias under multiple testing and for non-normal returns (skewness, kurtosis). When only one strategy was tried it reduces to the Probabilistic Sharpe Ratio. Implementations take the observed Sharpe, the number of trials, the variance of trial Sharpes, skew, kurtosis and the number of observations.

Vendors name survivorship and look-ahead bias as crypto backtest data pitfalls, without quantifying them. CoinAPI: survivorship bias 'occurs when your dataset only includes assets or markets that still exist today', covering delisted pairs, changed symbols, expired derivatives and shut-down venues; its fix is a point-in-time universe rebuilt at each date. Gainium: include failed assets (it cites Bitconnect and OneCoin), and do not alter a finished backtest with information unavailable at the time. Neither gives a number for the effect on returns or drawdown.

The Probability of Backtest Overfitting (PBO) is defined on the strategy-selection process: the probability that the configuration with the best in-sample performance ranks below the median of all N configurations out of sample. Combinatorially symmetric cross-validation (CSCV) estimates it from a T×N matrix of per-period returns, one column per trial, split into S blocks (the authors suggest S=16) with every half-in-sample, half-out-of-sample assignment scored. Minimum Backtest Length (MinBTL, Theorem 3.1 of the Notices paper) is the history in years needed so that the best of N independent zero-skill configurations has an expected in-sample annualised Sharpe of only 1. It equals the square of E[max of N standard normals] and is bounded above by 2 ln N. The paper's headline example: with 5 years of data, no more than 45 independent configurations should be tried 'or we are almost guaranteed' a strategy with in-sample Sharpe 1 and expected out-of-sample Sharpe 0; 7 trials need about 2 years. Galaxy (7 June 2024) says the trade needs significant capital for the spot purchase plus futures margin, and that the basis acts as a benchmark for short-term OTC crypto lending rates because lenders will not lend cash below the prevailing basis. That ties the basis level to financing costs for the spot leg.

DSR and PBO correct for selection bias; they do not audit the backtest itself. The PBO authors state the procedure 'does nothing to evaluate the correctness of a backtest' (their examples: wrong transaction costs, data not available at decision time), sees structural breaks only if they fall inside the sample, understates overfitting if trials are hidden, and can report a high PBO when many skilful strategies have similar Sharpe ratios. A forum post (snapshot dated 2026-04-03) describes a walk-forward-optimised crypto perpetual-futures bot with a backtest Sharpe of 1.1 to 2.7 that bled from the third live week. The author attributes it to three causes: searching thousands of parameter combinations and keeping the best; optimal parameters sitting on a cliff, where live spreads triggered the stop-loss on entry, which the backtest could not model; and an in-sample window that was an unusually stable volatility regime. This is one anecdote with no verified trade records.

The 2025-10-10 crash split liquidity providers by role. A simulated constant-spread maker lost heavily (Bieganowski and Slepaczuk). HLP, which also acts as the backstop liquidator, earned an estimated 40-41.5M USD that weekend. CoinGecko attributes that figure to liquidation-related income and does not separate it from market-making income. Datawallet puts the crash at about 19B USD of positions liquidated in 24 hours, over 10B USD of it on Hyperliquid. Reported profit in this case came from liquidation flow, not from spread capture.

Glassnode reports that the 3-month BTC futures basis has paid less than the 2-year U.S. Treasury yield since February 2026. Glassnode says only one earlier stretch on record ran as long (August 2022 to January 2023), and that stretch ended at the cycle low. TFTC (3 August 2026) and VT Markets (30 July 2026) both relay this single Glassnode report; neither gives an exact basis or yield.

Passive market makers lose money against informed (toxic) flow and earn the spread against uninformed flow. In a live 2024 Binance BTCUSDT-perp experiment the correlation between maker fill likelihood and post-fill returns was negative (fills come when price is about to move against the order). In a Binance Futures backtest to October 2025, a constant-spread maker was repeatedly filled on its bid in the 2025-10-10 flash crash and 'fell victim to severe adverse selection'.

Vendor and forum grid backtests are fragile. A Gainium user found a 2023-2025 backtest profit of 1,718 USD against about 362 USD from trade-count arithmetic. The vendor explained that when the start price sits inside the grid, the backtest assumes all base was bought at that start price (6.6) and credits initial sells against it, which inflates profit. For 2021-2025 the backtest (544 USD) matched the arithmetic (530 USD). If a grid result changes sharply with the start date alone, set an explicit start price so runs are comparable. Bieganowski and Slepaczuk backtest a signal-driven passive maker on Binance Futures perps (1-second data, 2022-01-01 to 2025-10-12). Costs include adverse selection but no taker fees and no stated maker rebate. BTC was strongest (ARC 2.93, MDD 0.38) but maker outperformance was not statistically significant for any asset (p>0.05; BTC p=0.1056); ENJ ARC was -0.81. The simulated maker 'suffered catastrophic losses' in the 2025-10-10 crash because its constant-spread logic did not widen.

Caporale and Plastun test BTC, LTC, XRP and DASH after price overreactions: the next-day move is larger in both directions, but a counter-movement (reversal) strategy was unprofitable and an inertia (momentum) strategy was profitable on paper yet statistically indistinguishable from random. The authors conclude the overreactions are not exploitable, possibly because of transaction costs.

Passive quotes earn the spread from uninformed flow and lose to informed flow. In a live 2024 experiment on the Binance BTCUSDT perpetual, Albers et al. found a negative correlation between a maker order's fill likelihood and its post-fill return, so fills tend to arrive just before price moves against the order. Multicoin Capital (2026-02-17) describes the same toxic-flow mechanism, and Bieganowski and Slepaczuk tie their 2025 crash result to Glosten-Milgrom adverse selection.

Chen et al. (arXiv 2506.11921) derive that a traditional grid has zero expected value when price moves up or down one step with equal probability, there are no fees, and all coins are sold if price falls below the grid. The derivation is theoretical; the paper does not test it empirically. The paper then proposes a Dynamic Grid Trading (DGT) variant that resets the grid to market conditions.

Queue position and cancel speed decide who captures the maker edge. In Albers et al. (large near-side queue, small opposite-side queue), the 1-second markout excluding rebate averaged -0.058 bp for front-of-queue fills and -0.775 bp for back-of-queue fills; when the queue was small, position mattered little. Multicoin says makers that cancel stale quotes first, segment flow or hedge fast can quote tighter, and credits Hyperliquid's rule that cancels execute before new taker orders for much of its liquidity.

Toxicity is a markout measured over an asset-dependent horizon. Multicoin says market makers judge flow over periods from microseconds up to about 10 minutes, and use longer windows for less liquid assets. Albers et al. measure post-fill returns with 1-second markouts and at 5 seconds after each order's terminal state.

Vine's cross-sectional variant (long low-funding, short high-funding perps, dollar-neutral, weekly) is the only funding strategy in that study to survive costs out of sample, and thinly: net Sharpe 0.71 in-sample, 0.39 purged walk-forward, deflated Sharpe 0.63, probability of backtest overfitting 0.81, max drawdown -35%, +1.7% through the Oct 2025 cascade window.

He, Manela, Ross and von Wachter find crypto perpetual futures deviate from no-arbitrage prices far more than in traditional currency markets (mean absolute deviation ~60-90% per year, 2020-01 to 2024-03) and that the implied arbitrage strategy earns net-of-fee Sharpe ratios of 1.80 (BTC, high retail fee tier) to 3.53 (BTC, no fees), with BTC net annualized excess returns of 6.4% (high fees) and ETH 9.6%.

The 21 Feb 2025 Bybit hack tested the model. LlamaRisk says about 20% of USDe collateral was hedged on Bybit perps. Ethena had under $30M of unrealized PnL on Bybit and cut it to zero within about two hours of the theft. USDe fell to about $0.96 on Bybit and $0.994 on the Curve USDC/USDe pool for about an hour, and the Chainlink USDe/USD feed hit $0.977. About $117M was redeemed through mint/redeem (redeem buffer raised to $250M). Six sUSDe liquidations on Aave totalled $22M with no bad debt. Independent measures put funding carry at roughly 8-13% a year through 2024: Ethena's docs report a 7.8-9% average for BTC/ETH funding over the three years before they were written (including the 2022 bear market); Vine's 30-coin Binance panel has a cross-sectional median of +7.3% (2023) and +13.4% (2024); and He et al. find an always-on BTC carry (long spot, short perp, 2020-01 to 2024-03, zero fees) earned 10.18% annualized excess return at 4.55% volatility (Sharpe 2.24, max drawdown -5.33%).

Hold-through delta-neutral positions need margin far above the initial stake in a rally: a TalTech bachelor-thesis backtest on Binance BTCUSDT (2019-12-23 to 2022-04-11, $10k spot + $10k short on $10k USDT collateral) shows $24.3k funding offsetting a roughly flat hedge P&L, yet a maximum unrealized loss of -$82.1k on the short; its 107.13% no-rebalance ROI equals profit divided by the initial $20k, while rebalanced variants (14-210 days) return 20-46%. Krestenko et al. address the same issue with a liquidation-probability budget and 5-10 rebalances over two years.

A retail-style Binance/Bybit funding-arb backtest (Oct 2023-Apr 2024, funding averaging 20-25% annualized) netted only $59 on $10,000 over 21 trades: $112.73 funding minus $56.70 fees, with four long-held SOL/ETH trades producing 69% of profit and short holds losing to ~0.27% round-trip fees; its figures do not reconcile and one-regime Sharpe 3.21 should not be extrapolated.

A retail-style Binance/Bybit funding-arb backtest (Oct 2023-Apr 2024, funding averaging 20-25% annualized) netted only $59.03 on $10,000 over 21 trades: $112.73 funding minus $56.70 fees (the figures do not reconcile), with four long-held SOL/ETH trades (168-232 hours) producing 69% of profit and short holds losing to fees; its Sharpe of 3.21 comes from one bull-market regime.

Funding extremes are capped differently by venue: Hyperliquid's docs (read 2026-11-06) cap funding at 0.5% per hour and call that much less aggressive than CEX caps, while He et al. report Binance adds an outer cap and floor of +/-3% for contracts with maximum leverage of 25x or below (tied to the maintenance margin ratio at 30x or above).

During the 2025-02-21 Bybit hack Ethena said all spot backing sat in off-exchange custody (Copper) and that Bybit hedge exposure was about $30M (Ethena, quoted by Chaos Labs and LlamaRisk, called it unrealized PnL), cut to zero within hours; LlamaRisk says about 20% of USDe's collateral backing was allocated to perp positions on Bybit. Open-source funding-arb backtesters are thin: perp-cli's backtest funding-arb command (PR 3, merged 2026-03-10) simulates a cross-venue perp-perp spread (hourly abs(rateA - rateB), annualized; defaults 30 days, enter at 10% and close at 5%, venues Hyperliquid and Pacifica), charges 0.1% per trade per leg, models no slippage and ignores the sign of each leg's payment; the sircharan/hype README (Hyperliquid HYPE spot-perp) states no results, period, fees, slippage or risks and needs a manually created CSV.

A public ML4T case study on 19 Binance perpetual futures (8-hourly bars, 2020-2025 history, two 1-year validation folds, 2 bps maker and 4 bps taker costs, official funding cash flows) selected the best of 2,807 candidate configurations. In its stored notebook output the selected validation Sharpe is 1.67, with a bootstrap 95% interval of 0.42 to 2.87 and a probabilistic-Sharpe p-value of 0.005. He, Manela, Ross and von Wachter's arbitrage rule (open when the futures-spot gap exceeds a no-arbitrage bound, close on convergence) earned BTC Sharpe 3.35 and 12.96% annualized excess return at the highest Binance retail fee tier, and 11.65 at zero fees; adding effective bid-ask spreads gives 3.27 and 10.46 (sample 2020-01-08 to 2024-03-11; v7 revised 2026-09-17). The authors also report that deviations from no-arbitrage prices diminish over time. Single paper, not independently replicated.

CMU's paper on Binance BTC perpetual contracts (8-hour funding data, 11 Aug 2020 to 20 Jun 2022) reports annualized carry-trade returns of 21.84% (Tether-settled, standard deviation 1.90%, Sharpe 11.5) and 16.74% (coin-settled, Sharpe 6.4) against a long-spot Sharpe of 0.41. Its main calculation abstracts from margin, leverage and transaction costs, and the paper quotes different Sharpe figures in its abstract (7 to 10), introduction (12.8 and 7.0) and Table 3. This is perpetual-funding carry, which overlaps the funding-rate sibling concept.

Funding carry compressed after the 2024 boom: Vine's 30-coin Binance panel shows median annualized funding of +13.4% (2024), +2.8% (2025) and +0.6% (Jan-May 2026); Stablecoin Insider (citing a Substack) puts BTC/ETH aggregate funding at about 11% in 2024 and 5% in 2025; and BitMEX's January 2026 year-end report says funding-rate arbitrage became crowded as exchange-native delta-neutral products expanded, with yields falling toward 4% and often below US Treasury rates by mid-2025.

Negative-funding evidence differs by scope: Ethena's docs say BTC/ETH funding was negative on 15.9% (BTC) to 17.5% (ETH) of days over the three years studied, the longest negative streak was 13 days, and only one quarter had a negative average combined return; LlamaRisk's venue-level data (June 2024) show single-venue negative episodes of 10 days at -46% annualized (Bybit), 13 days at -38% (Binance) and 24 days at -27% (OKX), and its stress case with 50% redemptions and a 20% LP discount still left reserves lasting 'at least four days'.

Funding carry compressed sharply after the 2024 peak. Median annualized funding across 30 Binance USD-M perps was 7.3% in 2023, 13.4% in 2024, 2.8% in 2025 and 0.6% in Jan-May 2026 (Vine). BTC averaged 3.99% annualized on Binance from 9 Dec 2025 to 13 Feb 2026 (askrubyai). A bot builder logged 1.2-1.8% average annualized rates on most Binance pairs for Nov 2025-May 2026. BitMEX says funding-arbitrage yields fell toward 4% and often below Treasury rates by mid-2025 as the trade crowded. The long-spot-only variant of the arbitrage (no spot shorting) still earns net Sharpe 1.62 for BTC and 2.23 for ETH at high fee tier, with BTC returns of 5.49%, so the retail-relevant version of the trade survives fees in the paper's 2020-2024 sample.

He, Manela, Ross and von Wachter (arXiv v7, 17 Sep 2026; sample from 8 Jan 2020 to 11 Mar 2024) derive no-arbitrage prices for perpetuals and test a random-maturity arbitrage that opens when the perp-spot gap exceeds the cost-implied bound. It earns a BTC Sharpe of 3.35 at the high retail fee tier (3.27 after effective bid-ask spreads) and up to 11.65 at zero fees, with mean absolute deviations of 52-90% a year. The earlier v5 reported BTC Sharpe 1.8 (high fees) and 3.5 (zero fees) and deviations of 60-90%, so the Sharpe level is unstable across versions. This is one research group.

Gate entries on fee break-even and persistence, because fees are fixed and funding spikes revert. A Binance bot builder found a $2.70 round-trip fee per $1,000 (0.27%) needs about 3.3 days at 30% annualized funding to break even, and that requiring 75% of the last 12 settlements above threshold removed 96% of entries. In its Oct 2023-Apr 2024 backtest four long holds (168-232 hours) made 69% of profit and short holds lost. Capacity is bounded by derivatives market size: in April 2024 Ethena's short ETH perp position was about 12% of ETH open interest ($9.75B), analysts warned that exchange position limits could cap USDe growth, and growth itself adds shorts that push funding down. Single source, 2024 data.

On 20 May 2026 AMBCrypto reported DeFi lending near 47.7% (about $2B) of backing and Ethena's share of crypto open interest at 0.05%. A single-asset EMA crossover with walk-forward tuning only matched buy-and-hold in a 21-month out-of-sample test at 0.1% per transaction, with lower drawdown and a higher information ratio. The authors' cost sweep (seven levels from 0.05% to 0.5%, positions held fixed) put break-even near 0.36% to 0.4% per transaction at 60-minute bars.

Average-cost models understate cost when it matters. Kaiko data (via CryptoSlate, April 2026) put BTC depth within 1% of mid at about $30 million on Binance, $16 to 20 million on Coinbase and $10 to 15 million on Gemini, Bybit and OKX, with weekday volume about double weekend volume; in March 2026 stress, the cost of trading BTC-USDT on Bybit rose 230%. AdaptiveTrend's authors say outages and flash crashes may produce slippage beyond their model. One practitioner post puts normal slippage on major pairs at 0.05% to 0.30% per trade and above 1% in news spikes (unverified).

Viable maker variants in the evidence are selective, rebate-dependent and low volume. Albers et al.'s profitable contrarian models fill 654-972 times per day against 15,380 for the naive maker, and they need a 0.5 bp rebate per leg. Shore's 2020 analysis found that his signal lifted the share of profitable liquidations to as high as 97% but cut volume sharply, and that BitMEX's 2.5 bp maker rebate with passive entry and exit turned a negative naive result into roughly +2 bp per position.

Historically, fee level sets the minimum profitable scale: on MtGox (2011-2013, 0.6% fee per trade) the authors state statistical arbitrage on Bitcoin is not profitable below the 60 bps fee level (120 bps round trip), and a separate Mt. Gox study finds non-expert arbitrageurs' trades become unprofitable once transaction costs are included. Today's fees are far lower, so this is a scale argument, not a current cost estimate.

The common 'cut the Sharpe ratio by 50%' rule is only a rule of thumb. Harvey and Liu (2015) show the multiple-testing haircut is nonlinear: under their assumptions it is almost always above 50%, sometimes far above, when annualized SR is below 0.4, and at most 25% when SR is above 1.0. In their 50-trial example the least profitable strategy (E/P, SR 0.43) lost almost 50% and the most profitable (betting against beta, SR 0.78) lost 7.9%. Method: convert SR to a t-ratio, adjust the p-value for N tests (Bonferroni, Holm or BHY), convert back; the percentage drop is the haircut. The DSR paper cal

Vendor grid profit figures often omit costs or depend on a hidden start price. A Gainium user found a 2023-2025 backtest showing $1,718 profit against about $362 from trade-by-trade arithmetic. A Gainium reply explained that the backtest started below the grid's top price, so every initial order was a sell and profit was measured from an assumed purchase price. Binance's futures-grid worked example gives about 0.93-1.02% profit per grid before fees and funding. Bitsgap's 513-bot replay leaves leverage, fees and funding as '[TBD]' in its own text.

The He and Manela edge is thin in dollar terms and faded after 2022. At high fees the Bitcoin strategy returns 6.38% a year in excess returns on 3.55% volatility, with a 4.43% maximum drawdown, and holds a position in only 20.06% of hours (average open-to-close time about 135 hours). Bitcoin annual returns are 8.29% (2020), 14.81% (2021), 0.28% (2022) and 1.11% (2023), with Sharpe ratios of 2.26, 2.39, 0.70 and 1.32. The authors report that futures-spot deviations became smaller and less volatile after 2022 and that the strategy became less active with lower returns. The sample ends in March 2

About 41% came from two events less than two weeks apart: the 2025-10-10 crash (about 41.5M USD in one weekend, roughly 10% for depositors) and a 2026-01-31 whale liquidation (about 15M USD, 5.8%). A 2021 test on 25 coins (30-minute bars, 1 July to 22 Nov 2021) found winners kept rising at steps above about 6 hours; a 24-hour-step momentum rule with 0.2% fees averaged +352% over simulated 100-day paths with annualised Sharpe above 3, and 5.99% of paths lost money. The evidence is weak. The sample is about 4.5 months of one bull run, the coins were chosen as large-cap names with full data at the time of writing (survivorship), windows overlap, and the paths come from i.i.d. resampling of bar returns, which removes autocorrelation and drawdown clustering. Albers et al. (live experiment, Binance BTCUSDT perp, 2024-02-12 to 02-19; 232,897 minimum-size maker orders): at the best fee tier (maker -0.5 bp rebate, taker 1.5 bp) the unconditional expected maker return is about -0.8 bp gross, -0.3 bp net of rebate, measured 5 s after order terminal state. Net of fees the naive maker averaged -0.43 bp and imbalance makers about -0.47 to -0.49 bp per roundtrip; an imbalance taker lost -1.96 bp. The paper says order-book mechanics render several commonly cited strategies 'highly unprofitable in practice'.

A 2021 30-minute-bar test of 25 coins found a 24-hour-step momentum strategy (0.2% fees) averaged about 352% over 100 simulated days with an annualised Sharpe above 3, but the Monte Carlo resampled a Jul-Nov 2021 bull-run sample; the author calls the sample short and the result preliminary.

Walk-forward with a single validation set can still overfit. A Columbia-led paper on deep-RL crypto trading frames overfitting detection as a hypothesis test on the PBO (alpha = 10%). Its results: conventional walk-forward PPO had PBO 17.5% (judged overfit), k-fold CV PPO 7.9%, and among agents PPO 8.0%, TD3 9.6% and SAC 21.3% (SAC rejected). The test window was only 2022-05-01 to 2022-06-27, so the performance comparison is short and the authors' own method.

In May 2024 the annualized front-month basis spiked above 25% for ETH and 19% for BTC after the SEC's ETH ETF announcement, then fell back. Galaxy notes the trade needs significant capital (spot purchase plus futures margin) and that the basis sets a floor for short-term OTC crypto lending rates, because lenders will not lend cash below the basis.

Basis spikes follow sentiment and regulatory catalysts. Galaxy reports that after the SEC's 20 May 2024 request for spot Ethereum ETF 19b-4 updates, the front-month annualized basis spiked above 25% for ETH and 19% for BTC before consolidating lower. CF Benchmarks reports the CME basis approached 25% in February 2024, exceeded 20% in November 2024, dipped below zero in March 2025 and was near 10% by May 2025, and says the basis is primarily driven by price momentum and sentiment (correlations of 0.50 and 0.54 with its two momentum proxies).

Evidence that cross-sectional momentum weakened after the 2021 bull market is thin and comes from low-authority sources. A February 2026 student backtest of 20-day cross-sectional momentum on 25 liquid coins found net Sharpe at 20 bps of 0.42 (2020 to 2022), -0.48 (2023 to 2024) and -2.18 (2025 to February 2026). Alpha t-statistics against BTC fell from 2.02 to 1.08 to -0.81. The author ties the fade to cross-sectional dispersion falling from 3.20% to 1.98%. Fieberg, Liedtke and Zaremba (2024) report that most abnormal returns of crypto anomalies arise in bull markets and fade over time (searc

The same perpetual-futures study finds mean absolute deviations from no-arbitrage prices of about 57-88% per year, and that deviations shrink about 11% per year; the authors describe the market as becoming more efficient. The edge available to a late entrant is therefore smaller than the sample-average Sharpe suggests.

Binance spot fees for a regular account are 0.100% maker and 0.100% taker, or 0.075% each when paid in BNB. VIP 1 (30-day volume of $1M or more and 5 BNB) pays 0.090% maker and 0.100% taker. VIP 5 pays 0.025% and 0.031%. VIP 8 pays 0.016% and 0.025%. VIP 9 pays 0.011% and 0.023%. VIP 1 maker with the BNB discount is 0.0675%, the 6.75 bps spot fee that He and Manela use for their high-cost case. The current VIP 5 and VIP 8 maker rates are below the 4.5 bps and 2.25 bps that paper used for its medium and low cases, so upper-tier fees have fallen since the paper's fee snapshot. Hyperliquid wallet data show who pays the costs on a perpetuals venue. Jia, Moallemi, Wang and Zeng studied 729,540 wallets on the ten busiest contracts from 27 March 2025 to 30 June 2026. They value each trade against the midprice 120 minutes later and subtract fees. Front-end traders, read as mostly retail, lost $1.11 billion: $154 million on voluntary trading, $226 million on net forced exits and $725 million in fees. Algorithmic market makers gained $208 million. Algorithmic takers roughly broke even. Front-end traders took liquidity on 85% of their volume against 20% for market makers, an

High carry has preceded crashes. BIS finds that a higher carry today predicts lower spot and futures prices at maturity (for 1-month BTC futures, a one-dollar rise in absolute carry predicts a five-dollar spot decline and a six-dollar futures decline), and that rising carry comes with a higher price of crash insurance in options. FTI reports perpetual funding rates climbed from about 10% to nearly 30% annualized by 6 October 2025, four days before the 10 October crash.

Competition erodes vault yields. Datawallet reports that Lighter's LLP vault (market making plus backstop liquidation) grew from about 20M USD in May 2025 to over 700M USD by the end of 2025 with APYs above 30%, and says much of that reflected fewer external market makers competing for the same trades. It expects returns to move toward HLP's range as professional market makers enter. This rests on one secondary page.

A strategy survives only if its gross edge per trade exceeds its all-in cost per trade, and break-even costs differ widely by strategy type. A walk-forward intraday EMA crossover on Bitcoin broke even near 0.36% (36 bps) per transaction. Hudson and Urquhart report average break-even costs from 7.88 bps (support-resistance rule, Litecoin) to 147.56 bps (filter rule, Ethereum), and as high as 66.41 and 57.51 bps for Bitcoin on two price series, against a Bitcoin cost of about 50 bps that they cite from earlier work. A trend system on 150+ perpetuals still showed a Sharpe ratio of 1.62 at 12 bps.

Albers et al. ran 232,897 minimum-size maker orders (127,051 filled) on 2024-02-12 to 2024-02-19 and assumed the most favourable Binance tier: maker -0.5 bp rebate, taker 1.5 bp. The unconditional expected maker return was about -0.8 bp gross and -0.3 bp net of rebate, measured 5 s after each order's terminal state. Net of fees per trade, the imbalance taker lost 1.96 bp (15 s hold), the naive maker 0.43 bp, the imbalance maker without cancel 0.47 bp and with cancel 0.49 bp. The paper reports a naive-maker Sharpe of -109. The authors say results would only deteriorate with less favourable fees

Venue fee tiers decide who can make money at the touch. Hyperliquid's base perps rate is 0.045% taker and +0.015% maker (1.5 bp, a cost). A maker rebate applies only to accounts that supply more than 0.5%, 1.5% or 3.0% of 14-day weighted maker volume, paying -0.001%, -0.002% or -0.003% (0.1 to 0.3 bp). Hyperliquid states it has no DMM program, special rebates or fees, or latency advantages. Albers et al. assumed a best-tier Binance rebate of 0.5 bp per leg, which is larger than Hyperliquid's deepest rebate.

Albers et al. ran a live experiment on Binance's BTCUSDT perpetual (continuous quoting 2024-02-12 to 2024-02-19; 232,897 minimum-size maker orders, 127,051 filled). At the best fee tier (maker rebate 0.5 bp, taker fee 1.5 bp) the unconditional expected maker return was about -0.8 bp, or -0.3 bp net of rebate, at a 5-second horizon. A naive quote-at-the-touch maker lost 0.44 bp per roundtrip net of rebates and, over about 3 days 7 hours, lost almost 60% with an annualized Sharpe of -109. The authors call the naive approach 'a quick path to bankruptcy' and say less favourable fee tiers would onl

Trend-style technical rules survive plausible costs in-sample, but out-of-sample evidence for Bitcoin is thin. Hudson and Urquhart report breakeven costs from 7.88 bps (support-resistance, Litecoin) to 147.56 bps (filter rule, Ethereum), and up to 66.41 and 57.51 bps for the two Bitcoin series, against about 50 bps typical Bitcoin trading cost they cite. After Bonferroni and Holm correction 33.61% of rules stay significant on the CoinDesk series. In the first half of 2018, a bear market, the best in-sample rules lost money on both Bitcoin series while the other three coins stayed positive. Fie

The expected maximum Sharpe ratio among strategies with no real edge rises with the number of trials N and falls with the length of history. A simulation of 1,000 zero-mean noise strategies on ten years of daily data gave a best-of-N mean annualised Sharpe of 1.03 (the winner exceeded 1.0 in 54.5% of runs). With three years of data and N=1,000 the expected maximum was 1.88. Best-of-100 averaged 0.79 and best-of-10 averaged 0.48.

Backtest-to-live degradation is large in the one multi-strategy study found, though not in crypto. Of 215 smart-beta strategies (average backtest 10.7 years, live 4.6 years), the median Sharpe haircut from backtest to live was 72% (80% for equity strategies), only 18 had a live Sharpe above the backtest, and 65 had a negative live Sharpe. The most complex strategies lost about 30 percentage points more than the simplest. The figures come from Bailey's blog summarising Suhonen, Lennkh and Perez (2017).

Suhonen, Lennkh and Perez (Journal of Portfolio Management, Winter 2017) compared backtests with live results for 215 bank-sponsored alternative-beta strategy indices (backtests averaged 10.7 years, live 4.6 years). The median Sharpe deterioration was 73% per the abstract as reported by Alpha Architect (72% in Bailey's summary, which also gives 80% for equity strategies). 65 of 215 (30%) had a negative live SR; only 18 (8.4%) did as well live as in the backtest; the most complex strategies lost over 30 percentage points more SR than the simplest. A high Sharpe from very few trades means nothing. Rulyfi found that unfiltered DSR > 0.95 flagged 8,449 strategies, all with 1 to 30 trades (8,420 with 1 to 10), because the skewness and kurtosis terms are noise at that size; it applies a 30-trade floor and calls that 'hygiene, not statistics'. Gainium suggests at least 100 trades as a rule of thumb. A dev.to BTC bot author's top-ranked strategy (SR 1.50, +546%) made two trades in three years and none in three months live. The 30 and 100 thresholds are heuristics, not derived from the DSR formula.

Per Glassnode data relayed by Cryptonomist (3 August 2026), the 3-month BTC futures basis yielded about 3% against about 3.8% on 2-year Treasuries, and had trailed Treasuries for 157 consecutive days since February 2026. The only comparable stretch was August 2022 to January 2023. The comparison pairs a 3-month basis with a 2-year yield (tenor mismatch), and the article's volume figures look unreliable.

Institutions run the trade as long spot-ETF shares (for example IBIT) against short CME bitcoin futures. CFTC data show hedge funds net short CME bitcoin futures. The Banque de France reads those shorts as ETF-futures arbitrage, not a bearish view, and cites a one-month basis of 0.3-0.8% (5-12% annualized) without stating the period. CF Benchmarks attributes leveraged funds' net short futures positioning after the ETF launch mainly to basis trades. The Block calls the CME-spot ETF basis trade the primary driver of institutional CME positioning (as of April 2026).

Glassnode data, relayed by TFTC and Cryptonomist on 3 August 2026, says the 3-month annualized BTC futures basis had paid less than the 2-year US Treasury since February 2026, and that only one other stretch on record ran this long (August 2022 to January 2023). Cryptonomist adds about 3% against about 3.8% and 157 consecutive days; TFTC gives no figures. Both articles rest on one Glassnode source (the Week 30 2026 'Paid to Wait' report and a Telegram post) that was not retrieved directly, and the comparison pairs a 3-month basis with a 2-year yield.

The only profitable maker variant in Albers et al. quotes against order-book imbalance (a balanced-inventory reversal model). With a logistic-regression threshold of 0.24 it earned +0.71 bp per roundtrip (standard deviation 13.69 bp, average hold about 268 s, Sharpe 11.97, p=0.0160); at threshold 0.26 it earned +1.21 bp (Sharpe 26.12, p=0.0303). Sharpe is annualized from hourly returns over only about 3.5 trading days, with minimum-size orders and the best possible 0.5 bp rebate. The authors say the Sharpe is unlikely to persist with larger orders, minor assumption changes could cut it sharply

Forum practitioners report a crypto backtest falling from +38% to flat once taker fees, slippage and funding were added, advise multiplying assumed fees and slippage by 2-4x, and flag perpetual funding payments, liquidation modelling and ambiguous intrabar stop/target ordering as common sources of inflated results.

A grid bot is a range and mean-reversion bet, and a sustained trend breaks it. In a downtrend it keeps buying, builds a growing long with negative unrealized PnL, and holds the full position once price falls below the lower bound. In an uptrend it sells out and sits flat, missing the rally. Bitsgap's replay shows the cost of a range that does not fit the market: 7 of its 8 liquidated futures replays were spot bots already losing 25% to 90%. Hummingbot's own Avellaneda-Stoikov guide gives the same inventory example for a symmetrical strategy in a BTC-USDT downtrend.

Gross short-horizon reversal in crypto is not tradable after realistic costs. A 25-coin, 30-minute test (July to November 2021) found 30-minute and 1-hour winners fall and losers rise. A Monte Carlo of the contrarian strategy with no costs averaged +298,900% in 100 days, but with a 0.1% fee on 4 trades per period it was unprofitable. A 25-coin daily test (2020 to February 2026) found 1-day reversal alpha with t = 4.64 in 2025 to February 2026 (gross Sharpe 4.41), but about 139% daily turnover turned net Sharpe to -1.73 at 20 bps one way; the README says it loses at any cost level, even 5 bps.

Harvey, Liu and Zhu (NBER w20592, RFS 2016) argued from a multiple-testing framework that a newly discovered equity factor should clear a t-ratio of 3.0, not 2.0. Andrew Chen (Federal Reserve Board, arXiv v10 dated 2025-11-19) disputes the claim that most findings are false: his simple bound gives a false discovery rate of at most 25% (eight of nine studies) and a refined bound about 9%. Both studies cover US cross-sectional equity predictors, not crypto, so the numbers do not transfer directly.

The claim that most published findings are false is contested. Chen (Federal Reserve Board, arXiv v10, 19 Nov 2025) bounds the false discovery rate of cross-sectional return predictors at 25% or less in eight of nine prior studies' summary statistics, and at 9% or less with a refined bound, and says the 'most are false' reading of Harvey-Liu-Zhu comes from treating insignificant factors as false discoveries. Jensen, Kelly and Pedersen (NBER w28432; Journal of Finance 2023) find the majority of asset pricing factors replicate, work out-of-sample in a new data set covering 93 countries, and have

Practitioner rule of thumb: model the exchange taker fee (about 0.10% unless high volume) plus at least 0.1-0.2% slippage per side; realistic costs reportedly cut backtest returns by 30-50%, and one backtest says slippage was about 63% of gross revenue for BTC low-frequency trend trading. These figures are unsourced author assertions, and the cited 1,243-post study could not be traced.

On-chain trading cost depends heavily on the token. Across 534,198 trades through the Uniswap Labs interface (January to mid-August 2023), the average cost per dollar was about 22 bps in the USDC-ETH pool and 140 bps in the PEPE-ETH pool; gas dominates small trades and slippage dominates large ones. A study of 4,990 DEX pairs on 27 chains (reported by CoinEdition, June 2026) puts round-trip costs at 230 to 240 bps against a best gross edge of about 6.5 bps per trade, with fewer than 1% of tested configurations profitable, liquidity-provision yield that disappears after impermanent loss, and cr

Retail-scale tests find almost no chart-based survivors. A freqtrade developer tested seven strategies on 24 months of Kraken data for ten USD pairs at 0.25% maker and 0.40% taker fees. All seven lost money, from -1.16% (5 trades) to -95.48% (a grid bot that won 93.3% of its 608 trades), while the BTC-led basket fell 13% to 18%; the author blames exit logic more than fees. Gatto's 4,990-pair DEX study likewise found fewer than 1% of configurations profitable, and says most signals were too weak even before fees.

A practitioner post advises testing with the exchange taker fee (about 0.10%) plus at least 0.1% to 0.2% slippage per side, says realistic costs cut reported returns by 30% to 50%, and says the author's bot lost money for four months live after a backtest of 240% a year. These are unsourced author assertions.

BIS Working Paper 1087 (Schmeling, Schrimpf, Todorov, 4 April 2023) finds crypto carry (the futures-spot gap) for Bitcoin and Ethereum averages above 10% a year and reaches up to 60% a year, much larger than carry in equities, bonds, FX or commodities.

A cash-and-carry trade buys the spot asset (or a spot ETF) and sells an equal notional of futures. The futures price converges to spot at expiry, so the trader keeps the entry basis as profit. The usual quote is annualized basis = (F - S) / S x 365 / days to expiry. A 3% basis on a 90-day contract is 12.2% annualized.

Time-series (per-asset trend) momentum tends to beat cross-sectional momentum in small crypto universes. Han, Kang and Ryu report strong time-series but weak cross-sectional momentum, concentrated in bull markets. A 2026 test on 8 coins (2020 to Oct 2025) with volatility-normalised multi-horizon EMAs found time-series momentum returned 31.96% a year while cross-sectional momentum had a 55.0% maximum drawdown, which the author links to high cross-coin correlation. The 2026 abstract does not state whether costs were charged.

Cross-sectional momentum weakens in later samples in two independent tests. Grobys et al. find the top-30-coin payoff averaged 1.74% per week (10% significance) through July 2020, then a negative, insignificant average in the August 2020 to December 2023 subsample, which the authors attribute to the single December 2020 crash week. A 25-coin daily 20-day-momentum test at 20 bp one-way found net Sharpe 0.42 (2020-2022), -0.48 (2023-2024) and -2.18 (2025 to 5 Feb 2026), with BTC-alpha t-stats of 2.02, 1.08 and -0.81 and a breakeven cost near 35 bp in a full-period sweep; its author ties the deca

Published studies assume very different costs, and the cost model decides the verdict. Assumptions: Binance maker fees of 1.44 bps (perpetuals) and 6.75 bps (spot) at the high-cost VIP 1 tier (He et al.); a 4 bps taker fee plus modelled slippage and funding (AdaptiveTrend); 10 bps (Zarattini et al., who say typical Bitcoin costs are below 5 bps); 8 bps per round trip (Pindza and Mba); 15 bps per half-turn (Fischer et al., 2018 data); 13 bps one-way (Bakker, 2017 Bitstamp tier). A retail bot developer quoted base-tier fees in May 2026 of 0.25% maker and 0.40% taker on Kraken, and 0.4% maker and

Turnover control is the documented lever against costs. Zarattini et al. report that a 20% rebalance threshold, applied only to volatility-driven rebalances, recovers roughly 100 bps a year at the 50 bps cost level. In AdaptiveTrend (net of 4 bps), 1-hour candles gave Sharpe 1.54 with 847 trades a month and 412% turnover, while 6-hour candles gave Sharpe 2.41 with 142 trades a month and 134% turnover.

Published crypto market-making studies often use short samples and leave out frictions. Sadighian (2019) tests deep-RL agents on Coinbase data for two days (2019-11-01 and 11-02), models no maker fees or rebates and charges market orders 0.20% per side. Wang, Ventre and Polukarov test on simulated Brownian prices with no transaction costs, rebates or adverse-selection signals. Albers et al.'s profitable variant covers about 3.5 trading days with a best-case rebate.

A 2026 preprint on volatility-scaled monthly time-series momentum (BTC, ETH, two spot Bitcoin ETFs, GLD and SPY; January 2018 to March 2026) reports an annualised return of 18.03% and Sharpe 0.82 before the first US spot Bitcoin ETF (11 January 2024) and 28.58% and 1.22 after. The difference is not statistically significant (p = 0.5835), and the abstract does not say whether costs were charged. The authors conclude time-series momentum is most useful in uncertain, regime-switching conditions after institutional entry.

The Liu-Tsyvinski-Wu momentum returns are gross of trading costs and assume the loser quintile can be shorted; the paper itself says short selling is either not possible or limited for most coins. When the short leg is replaced by Bitcoin, only the 3-week strategy stays significant (3.0% per week, t=2.25); the 1-, 2- and 4-week strategies fall to 0.9%, 1.8% and 1.4% per week with t-stats of 0.69, 1.50 and 1.20. The sample's median coin has an $8.17M market cap and about $104K of daily dollar volume. Begusic and Kostanjcar restrict their tradable portfolios to long-only because shorting opportu

A 2026 developer post-mortem tested seven strategies over 24 months at Coinbase Advanced Trade (0.4% maker, 0.6% taker) and Kraken Pro (0.25% maker, 0.40% taker) fees. None cleared the author's bar of net 1.5% a month. The best result was -17.75% (Fear and Greed without a stop-loss, 15 trades). A grid bot lost 95.48% over 608 trades despite a 93.3% win rate. The author blames exit logic ('the exit logic dominates the entry logic'), not fees, and does not state a slippage assumption. This is one developer's anecdote over a market the author says fell 13-18%.

Bitsgap (vendor, 2026-10-05) replayed 513 real spot grid bots (each ran over 7 days on real funds) as long futures grids over the same dates. Futures finished ahead in 370 (72.1%). Average ROE was +9.7% against +1.6% on spot, and the median was +8.5% against +1.5%. Eight replays (1.6%) were liquidated, 7 of them in bots already down 25% to 90% on spot. Four bots that made +100% to +200% on spot finished between about +33% and +105% on futures. Leverage is unstated, results are a backtest, and Bitsgap sells futures grid bots.

A systematic crypto trader reports a bot whose backtest showed 240% a year lost money live for four months, which they trace to unmodeled slippage (0.05-0.30% per trade on major pairs, over 1% in news spikes) and a taker fee near 0.10%. Their rule of thumb is to re-run any backtest with the taker fee plus at least 0.1-0.2% slippage per side, and to expect that strategies which hold up trade less and hold longer. The article's cited study of 1,243 forum posts (57% of failures from slippage) and its 30-50% return haircut have no traceable source.

A completed-cycle win rate says nothing about total grid return. Binance reports Grid Profit (realized buy-sell pairs) separately from unrealized Float Profit, so open inventory sits outside completed-cycle statistics. The Solana grid post advertises a '100% win rate on completed grid cycles' next to +11.7% in a backtest during a 37% SOL drop, without reporting open positions.

A bootstrapped Monte Carlo on a short bull-run sample can manufacture an edge. A 2021 blog test resampled per-period returns from a July to November 2021 sample of 25 coins. It reported 24-hour winner-momentum averaging +352% in 100 days at 0.2% round-trip cost, an annualised Sharpe above 3 and 5.99% of paths losing money. The author calls the sample short and the result preliminary and doubts that overlapping windows are valid. Treat this as an illustration of sample dependence, not as a tradable edge.

Hummingbot's pure market making strategy cancels and replaces its quotes every order_refresh_time seconds. Inventory skew is off by default (target 50% base, range multiplier 50 when enabled). Orders are replaced after max_order_age (default 1800 s) and filled_order_delay defaults to 60 s. The strategy page lists price floor and ceiling and minimum_spread controls but no stop-loss or kill switch, and it makes no performance claims.

Crypto momentum is exposed to crashes and a few extreme periods. A 2025 Springer paper reports one outlier equals 37% of the strategy's compounded return, with a December 2020 crash of -255.23%. A University of Vaasa working paper reports plain momentum is profitable only after trimming and remains highly sample-dependent even then. Both claims were read through search-engine summaries, not full text.

Dobrynskaya's 'Cryptocurrency Momentum and Reversal' (Journal of Alternative Investments 26(1), 2023, pp. 65-76) sorts about 2,000 coins above $1M market cap (2014-2020) into top-30% and bottom-30% portfolios, with lookbacks from 1 week to 2 years and holding periods of 1-12 weeks. Funding-only Sharpe ratios (e.g. 18.15 on 66 days of Binance BTC funding) measure funding variance alone and exclude basis, liquidation, exchange and slippage risk, so they overstate risk-adjusted return; 'true' strategy Sharpe in that source is an unsupported 1-3 estimate.

Funding-only Sharpe ratios are artefacts of funding's low variance: Vine's cash-and-carry harvest on 30 Binance perps (Jan 2023-May 2026, 6 bp per side; single venue, survivorship-biased universe, spot used as perp proxy) posts Sharpe 8.5 but only +5.6% a year net, decaying to negative in 2026 (below the ~5% risk-free rate), because a funding-only model omits basis blow-outs, liquidation and de-peg tails; askrubyai's 66-day Binance BTCUSDT sample shows annualized Sharpe 18.15 at 3.99% APY and guesses a 'true' Sharpe of 1-3 without evidence.

BIS attributes crypto carry to a volatile convenience yield from two forces: trend-chasing small investors who want leveraged long exposure, and scarce, slow-moving arbitrage capital. Interest-rate differentials explain little of the variation; even Binance VIP borrow rates are too low to account for the average carry. The CMU study of Binance perpetuals (Aug 2020 to Jun 2022) agrees on the mechanism: the carry trade earns because longs pay for leverage, and its returns dropped after Binance cut maximum leverage from 125x to 50x in July 2021.

Hedged carry positions can show losses in a selloff. When spot falls faster than futures and the basis compresses, the long spot leg loses more than the short futures leg gains. Risk limits then force unwinds (sell spot, buy futures), which adds downward pressure. Kaiko/Amberdata links part of the October 2025 ETF outflows to such arbitrage unwinds.

Documented risk controls for grid and maker bots exist, but none of the sources measures whether they preserve profit. Hummingbot's guide lists inventory skew, filled-order delay, hanging orders, ping-pong mode and asymmetric spreads. The Gate.io practitioner uses an external drawdown stop (close and reassess when unrealized loss passes a set share of margin), 2x or lower leverage, wide ranges, and margin-ratio alerts at under 10% with a hard pause at under 5%. Binance recommends setting stop-trigger orders in advance.

The trade is risk-free only at convergence. While it is open the basis can widen, for example when trend followers add long futures, so the short leg shows mark-to-market losses, draws margin calls and can be liquidated before maturity even though the trade would have paid at expiry. Practitioner sources describe the same 'right but early' problem and add exchange counterparty risk, perpetual funding swings and slippage at scale. CryptoSlate says calling the trade 'riskless' overstates it.

Perpetual-futures grids add funding payments and liquidation on top of trend risk. A Gate.io practitioner cut leverage from 5x to 2x after concluding that a 20% drop against an accumulated long would liquidate the account, and paid funding while full-long in a downtrend. Bitsgap's replay liquidated 8 of 513 bots, and 7 of those 8 were already losing 25-90% on spot.

BIS states cash-and-carry is risky because margins spike and positions can be liquidated during drawdowns. This is a limit to arbitrage and lets high carry persist. Practitioner explainers describe the same 'right but early' failure: the basis can widen before it converges, and a margin call can force an exit at a loss even though the trade would have paid at expiry.

Backtest overfitting is trying too many variations of a strategy on the same historical data relative to the amount of data. It is an instance of multiple testing. Standard overfitting controls fail to detect it because they assume a single test was run.

The trade's economic viability is judged against the risk-free rate plus capital and counterparty costs, not against zero. The Block frames the trade as unattractive once basis yield falls below the risk-free rate plus those costs. Kaiko/Amberdata likewise proposes staying in T-bills when its carry score is low. Gross basis alone overstates net return.

The long spot leg usually cannot collateralize the short futures leg. On CME the spot cannot be held at the exchange, so short-futures losses are not offset automatically by spot gains. BIS adds that some exchanges use USD as the margin numeraire, so meeting a margin call means selling spot, which removes the hedge. A Sharpe ratio is itself a noisy estimate. Under IID Normal returns the annualised estimate is asymptotically Normal with variance (1 + SR²/2q)/y for y years and q observations per year (Lo 2002), so with a true Sharpe of zero its standard error is 1/√y. A year of daily data gives a standard error of about 1, and a backtested Sharpe of 1 on one year cannot be told from zero. The ML4T script adds that quoting a Sharpe without its sample length makes it uninterpretable, and that assuming normality on a fat-tailed series understates the uncertainty in the direction that flatters the strategy.

Cash-and-carry means long spot (or a spot ETF) plus short a dated future. If the future trades above spot, the premium is the locked-in profit, and it converges to zero at expiry. CME bitcoin futures are cash-settled against a reference rate, so the spot leg is never delivered. Position P&L equals the premium captured minus any widening of the basis before expiry (P&L = minus the change in futures-minus-spot), so basis compression helps the holder and basis widening hurts. The P&L identity is a derivation consistent with BIS's description of the risk.

In 2025 the 30-day annualized BTC basis averaged about 5.0% (7-day 4.4%, 90-day 6.8%) after a January peak of 15.3% (7-day 22.2%). Against an assumed constant 4.5% T-bill rate, excess return was positive on 177 of 365 days (48%), and by quarter +2.6, -1.0, 0.0 and +0.6 percentage points. In April 2026 The Block reported about 5% basis against about 4.5% risk-free, and CME bitcoin futures average daily open interest of $7.2 billion, the lowest since February 2024.

Leveraged perpetual grids add liquidation and funding risk on top of trend risk. The Gate.io practitioner ran 5x, found a sustained move liquidation-prone (later cut to 2x), and paid funding during a downtrend on top of unrealized losses. Bitsgap's replay also saw 8 futures-grid liquidations, mostly of bots already deep underwater.

The Deflated Sharpe Ratio paper says the most important information missing from virtually all published backtests is the number of trials attempted, and that a backtest whose search extent was not controlled is 'worthless, regardless of how excellent the reported performance might be'. The long-form Notices paper says published backtests almost never declare the number of trials. An independent open-source lesson makes the same operational point: statistics computed on the selected strategy cannot see the search, so the number of candidates tried must be reported.

Cross-exchange spreads persist because arbitrage capital is scarce and constrained, not because they are cheap to capture: Makarov and Schoar link large recurrent deviations to capital controls and slow-moving capital, and report within-country deviations that typically do not exceed 1%; the BIS paper likewise attributes carry to the scarcity of arbitrage capital.

Avellaneda-Stoikov (A&S) is the inventory-risk market-making model that Hummingbot implements. The original model assumes a finite trading session, and Wang et al. note that A&S-style models assume the maker knows the stochastic dynamics of the state variables. Hummingbot adapts the model to 24/7 markets with a user-set session length. Because the paper gives no way to calculate risk aversion (gamma) or order-book depth (kappa), Hummingbot's easy mode estimates both from spread limits. Neither Hummingbot A&S page presents backtests, fees or adverse-selection analysis.

Popular failure-rate claims are unsourced, and two practitioner posts in the evidence set are promotional. The TrendRider article's headline that 90% of bots fail and its win rates (60-80% for market making, 40-60% for trend following) cite no data. Its loss example is internally inconsistent (a 0.1 BTC order against a 3,000 USD loss on a 5% BTC drop), and the author promotes his own trend-following bot. The Gate.io grid write-up first appeared on a vendor blog, ends with a pitch for the GridLens monitoring product, and labels its own PnL as illustrative.

A grid bot places buy and sell limit orders at fixed price steps inside a chosen range and books about one step of profit per completed buy-then-sell cycle. Exchanges position it for sideways markets: Binance says spot grid suits assets that fluctuate within a stable range, and a Gate.io practitioner says the bot earns only while price stays inside the band. In a Gainium forum worked example, a 41-level grid on 600 USD with 1.89% spacing earned about 0.26 USD per sell on 14 USD per level.

Multicoin lists six levers venues use to cut adverse selection for passive liquidity: delay execution, hide intent, segment flow, price risk dynamically, refuse flow in some conditions, and social coordination. It credits Hyperliquid's cancel-first 'maker priority' with letting makers quote tighter, and says Binance followed Paradex's retail price improvement model for futures. Multicoin has portfolio ties to firms it cites, such as DFlow. Hyperliquid's own order-book page states only price-time priority, so the cancel-first claim is uncorroborated.

A grid bot buys at preset levels below the market and sells at the next level above, so it earns only while price stays inside its range. If price falls through the range, the bot holds the full position at an unrealized loss. If price rises through the range, the bot sells out and misses the move. Binance's documentation reports Total Profit as Grid Profit (completed buy-sell pairs, fees already deducted) plus unrealized Float Profit, and warns that bots keep executing during a sharp collapse. A practitioner write-up and Hummingbot's inventory-risk guide describe the same trend failure.

Plain cross-sectional momentum in large crypto coins carries single-coin crash risk. The raw payoff is 1.74% a week to July 2020 (significant at 10% only) and 0.90% a week overall (insignificant). A passive market maker earns the spread from uninformed flow and loses to informed flow, and a trending market leaves it holding a falling asset. Four independent sources agree on this mechanism: Multicoin Capital (industry essay, 2026), Hummingbot's inventory-risk guide (practitioner documentation), the Albers et al. live Binance experiment, and Cekal's 2026 simulation-plus-historical study, in which inventory revaluation outweighed spread capture.

Short holding periods fail first when costs rise. At 50 bps, the 5-day Donchian Bitcoin model in Zarattini et al. falls from 34% to 18% CAGR, and longer-lookback models fall less. At 0.1% per transaction, Mroziewicz and Ślepaczuk find 1- to 15-minute EMA-crossover intervals likely unprofitable and advise against intervals below 60 minutes. In Bakker's 5-minute BTC/USD study (2013 to 2017), the best pre-cost rule broke even at 6.32 bps one-way against a 10 bps minimum Bitstamp fee, and at 13 bps one-way only 22 of 3,312 rules stayed significant after data-snooping control (541 before costs).

Funding-only Sharpe ratios mislead because funding is a smooth stream. Vine's delta-neutral level harvest on 30 Binance perps shows Sharpe 8.5 but only +5.6% a year net over 2023-2026, decaying year by year to negative in 2026, when it no longer beats the ~5% risk-free rate. askrubyai's 66-day BTC sample gives Sharpe 18.15 on $72.84 of PnL on $10,000. A Binance bot backtest gives Sharpe 3.21 in one 20-25% funding regime. None models basis blowouts, liquidations, exchange loss or slippage, so report net return instead of Sharpe.

Perpetual-versus-spot basis capture is the best-documented survivor at retail-level fees. He et al. report a BTC Sharpe of 1.8 using Binance maker fees for the high-cost tier (6.75 bps spot, 1.44 bps perpetual), and up to 3.5 with zero fees. Their Kaiko order-book sample puts the BTC perpetual spread below 0.05 bps and the price impact of a 0.5 million trade below 0.3 bps, so direct fees dominate costs. Perpetual-vs-spot basis arbitrage is the strongest net-of-cost result found: using Binance maker fees for the individual-trader tier (0.0675% spot / 0.0144% futures) and sub-0.35 bps combined spread and impact, the simulated strategy has a BTC Sharpe of 1.80 (3.53 with zero fees); ETH 2.55, BNB 4.84. The BIS carry paper nonetheless warns that the matching cash-and-carry position is risky because of margin spikes and liquidations in drawdowns.

AMBCrypto (2026-05-20), citing Ethena's transparency dashboard, reports USDe backing of about 47.7% DeFi lending (~$2B) and 52.7% liquid stablecoins (the source's figures sum above 100%), with institutional lending and crypto basis exposure only 'a small fraction', a 101.55% backing ratio, ~$4.45B supply, Ethena at 0.05% of total crypto open interest, and sUSDe APY near 4% against average funding near 6.8%. If accurate, USDe in 2026 earns mostly credit and stablecoin yield rather than perp-funding carry. Not corroborated: Ethena's dashboard could not be read.

The same trade earns different carry on different venues. BIS finds carry is correlated above 90% across crypto-native exchanges but only about 60-70% between them and CME, and reports initial margin under 2% on crypto-native exchanges versus 50% on CME. Diversified, low-turnover trend following reports positive net results, but only as author backtests. Zarattini et al.: a monthly-rebalanced, volatility-sized portfolio of the 20 most liquid coins earned a net Sharpe of 1.57, a maximum drawdown of 11% and an 11% alpha versus Bitcoin at 10 bps with a 20% rebalance threshold (backtest 1 January 2015 to 19 March 2025). AdaptiveTrend: Sharpe 2.41 net of a 4 bps taker fee, modelled slippage and funding on 150+ Binance perpetuals (out of sample 2022 to 2024), falling to 2.01 at 8 bps and 1.62 at 12 bps.

Funding carry compressed sharply in 2025-26: Ethena's yield feed shows BTC/ETH aggregate funding averaging ~11% annualized in 2024 and ~5% in 2025, and sUSDe paying 4.75% (30-day avg 4.74%, 90-day avg 4.53%) on 2026-10-14 versus a ~10.34% since-inception average; an independent Binance BTCUSDT sample (Dec 2025-Feb 2026) averaged ~4% annualized funding.

In the same paper's return decomposition (BTC, zero-fee tier, annualized %), 37.61 points of the 52.55 total come from price convergence and 14.94 from funding payments; funding was the larger leg only in 2024 (18.15 versus 3.30), while price convergence dominated 2020-2023. The paper reports its dynamic rule beats the always-on carry (BTC zero-fee Sharpe 11.65 versus 2.24), so most of the historical edge came from trading dislocations, not from simply collecting funding.

Funding backtests break on data hazards: Vine masked MATIC funding after the MATIC-to-POL rename (~2024-09) because funding was pinned to the exchange default, and summed TIA's 4-hour settlements to a daily grid (other contracts settle every 8 hours); jyotirmoy17 found live WebSocket funding updates written with current timestamps contaminated the 8-hourly history (82 false consecutive elevated ticks), a persistence-scorer warm-up returned 100% persistence after one observation, and the backtest engine hardcoded a window size (24 instead of 12) so no trades fired.

Open-source audit tooling exists but is small and unvalidated here. Cross-exchange gaps exist, but few traders capture them. Makarov and Schoar document large, recurrent price gaps across exchanges, much larger across countries than within them, and link them to capital controls. In Mt. Gox data (2011 to early 2014), Saggese et al. split 440 arbitrageurs by single versus multiple markets as a proxy for ability: the group their abstract labels 'expert' lost money on average after transaction costs, while 'skilled' investors earned a significant positive premium, and order splitting and non-aggressive trading raised profit. BIS Working Paper 1087 finds crypto carry averaged about 10% a year across exchanges from April 2019 to January 2022. Carry exceeded 40% a year on crypto-native exchanges in several spikes (the abstract says up to 60%), reached about 30% on CME in early 2021, and fell below -20% at the low. CMU's Binance data show a default perpetual funding rate of 0.01% per 8 hours, about 11% a year, and find that funding rather than basis change drives the mean return of the perpetual carry trade.

Published 'basis versus Treasury' comparisons are not like-for-like. Glassnode's compares a 3-month basis with a 2-year Treasury (TFTC). Kaiko/Amberdata subtracts a constant 4.5% T-bill rate for all of 2025. The Block's 'about 4.5% risk-free' is not identified as a T-bill. CryptoSlate uses the 2-year par yield (4.19% on 7 August 2026) while the analyst it rebuts used 3.8%. Whether the trade 'beats Treasuries' therefore depends on the tenor match, the venue and contract, and whether costs are netted.

Bitsgap (vendor, published 2026-10-05) replayed 513 real spot grid bots as long futures grids over the same dates: futures finished ahead in 370 (72.1%), average ROE +9.7% vs +1.6% on spot, median +8.5% vs +1.5%, 8 liquidations (1.6%), 7 of which were already losing 25-90% on spot. Leverage, fees and funding are unstated, results are a backtest, and the sample is only bots that ran over 7 days on real funds.

One practitioner's grid guardrails (anecdotal, single source): block new orders when free balance falls under a threshold (about 40 USDT for roughly 10 concurrent grids), warn at margin ratio below 10% and hard-pause below 5%, add an external drawdown stop, use wide ranges rather than tight ones, and keep leverage at 2x or lower. Tight ranges raised fee bleed and left the bot idle outside the range for two weeks after a 3,000 USD daily move.

Diversified, volatility-sized trend following on a survivorship-bias-free universe (rotational top-20 liquid coins, Donchian ensemble) reports a net-of-fees Sharpe above 1.5 and 10.8% annualized alpha versus Bitcoin, whereas a single-asset EMA crossover with walk-forward tuning matched but did not beat buy-and-hold on Sharpe for BTC, ETH and BNB at 10 bps per transaction (breakeven about 36-40 bps).

Hedge funds cut ETF positions as carry fell in late 2025. CF Benchmarks reports that the top hedge-fund holders of IBIT cut holdings from about 114 million shares in Q3 2025 to 82 million in Q4 2025 (-28%), including Brevan Howard from 37.5 million to 5.5 million shares. It attributes the cuts to the October 2025 blow-off top and the basis compression that followed. Kaiko/Amberdata and Spark likewise attribute part of the Q4 2025 ETF outflows to basis-trade unwinds rather than directional selling, but none of the three sources measures that share.

Short-horizon reversal is statistically real but does not clear costs at the horizons where it appears. A 2021 test on 25 coins found 30-minute and 1-hour winners fell and losers rose, yet contrarian trading lost money after 0.1% fees on four trades per period. Practitioner screens for overfitting, not validated by the academic sources here: perturb each parameter by 10 to 20% and expect smooth degradation rather than a cliff (TrendRider); validate across bull, bear, sideways, high-volatility and low-volatility regimes (TrendRider); treat 'works only on one symbol, one period or one exact parameter set' as a warning sign (MQL5 blog); double the assumed commission and slippage and drop strategies that fail (dev.to author). Chen reports that close-in-time out-of-sample tests show decay of about 20% to 36% in published predictor returns, and broader samples show decay up to 60% which he attributes largely to economic rather than statistical causes. His 'true discovery' means statistically significant nonzero alpha only; trading costs and arbitrage limits are not modelled, and net-of-cost profits for most findings are small.

Cross-sectional momentum on 25 liquid coins decayed out of sample: net Sharpe at 20 bps was 0.42 (2020-2022 training), -0.48 (2023-2024 validation) and -2.18 (2025 to Feb 2026). Alpha t-stats vs BTC fell from 2.02 to 1.08 to -0.81. The author attributes the decline to cross-sectional dispersion dropping from 3.20% to 1.98% after 2023.

Vendor and forum grid backtests are fragile and often under-specified. A Gainium forum user found a 2023-2025 backtest showing $1,718 profit versus about $362 from trade-by-trade arithmetic; the vendor attributed the gap to the backtest's start price, which made initial sell orders profit against an assumed purchase price. For automated market makers the same trade-off is formal. Liquidity-provider returns split into a market-beta part and an alpha equal to fees earned minus losses to arbitrageurs (loss-versus-rebalancing). For the Uniswap v2 ETH-USDC pool, over 99.991% of LP return variance came from market beta. Multicoin likewise calls AMM arbitrage inherently adverse selection for market makers. This is an adjacent venue type, not a limit-order-book grid.

Outside crypto, short-term trend following can decay for microstructure reasons rather than regime alone. A July 2026 preprint (Kurth, Eisler, Rej and Bouchaud) uses about 100 liquid futures contracts from 1995 to 2025. It finds short-term trend returns stopped being reliable from about 2009, with the loss concentrated in small-tick contracts and trend intact in large-tick ones. It argues that high-frequency market making breaks the price-impact loop that sustains trend. The text contains no crypto data, so it is a scoping note, not crypto evidence.

Queue position and speed decide maker edge. In the Binance BTC-perp experiment, average markout in the large-near-queue / small-opposite-queue case was -0.058 bp for front-of-queue fills versus -0.775 bp for back-of-queue fills, and fill probability ranged from about 30% to over 90% depending on queue imbalance. Multicoin likewise says makers that cancel stale quotes first, segment flow, or hedge fast can quote tighter, and that HFT firms spend millions on data and research that average traders do not.

Cekal (FFA Working Paper 4/2026, May 2026) splits market-making PnL into trade edge and inventory revaluation. On one 46-minute BTC perpetual window (2021-10-03 21:00-21:46), a baseline that quotes near the market earned +$15.9 of trade edge but -$238.6 of inventory fluctuation, net -$222.7. The PPO policy quoted wider ($6.65 vs $1.84), cut mean absolute inventory from 0.189 to 0.067 contracts, and still lost $62.0. On ETH the trade edge was about equal (-$1.0 vs -$1.3) and inventory fluctuation drove a -$13.5 vs -$218.6 gap. The author calls the historical screens 'diagnostic' rather than sta

Auto-deleveraging (ADL) can break the hedge. BitMEX says ADL mechanisms on several exchanges disrupted delta-neutral strategies in the 10-11 Oct 2025 crash (about $20B of liquidations) and forced professional market makers to cut liquidity. Chitra's arXiv paper finds Hyperliquid used ADL to close $2.1B of positions in 12 minutes and that Binance used ADL far more than Hyperliquid. Hyperliquid's Jeff Yan says ADL closed profitable short positions at favorable prices. A short perp leg profits in a crash, so ADL closing it can leave the spot leg unhedged (inference from these descriptions).

Binance's public futures API (/fapi/v1/fundingRate) returns 8-hour funding history (askrubyai pulled 200 observations), and Binance's public data archive supplied Vine's 112,853-observation panel. Backtests of funding strategies are prone to data bugs: mixing live WebSocket intra-period funding updates with the 8-hourly settlements (00:00/08:00/16:00 UTC) contaminated history, and a persistence-scorer warm-up artefact triggered false entries until fixed.
