facts.text: Public evidence that retail grid bots beat buy-and-hold net of realistic costs is weak. It rests on an author-run preprint with in-sample backtests and no slippage (Chen et al.), a vendor replay with unstated leverage and fee assumptions (Bitsgap), and a student project that does not discuss fees and found ML-tuned grids no better than plain grids (Stevens Hanlon FSC, 2024-10-22). A fourth item, a self-published 17-coin walk-forward study (YodaCom Paper 1, May 2026), was withdrawn in October 2026 pending a simulator rebuilt with stricter assumptions. Its publisher also sells a crypto product.

Minimum Backtest Length (MinBTL): to hold the expected best in-sample SR of N skill-less strategies at E[max_N], the backtest must run at least [(1-g) Phi^-1(1-1/N) + g Phi^-1(1-1/(N e))]^2 / E[max_N]^2 years; the authors' simple upper bound is 2 ln(N) / E[max_N]^2. Their headline cases, with E[max_N] = 1 and expected out-of-sample SR 0: 5 years of data supports no more than 45 independent configurations, and 7 configurations already reach in-sample SR 1 on a 2-year backtest. Recomputed here from the formula: N=45 needs 5.0 years, N=100 needs 6.4 years, N=1,000 needs 10.6 years. The authors ca

Exchange auto-deleveraging (ADL) can close the profitable hedge leg. FTI reports that on 10 October 2025 ADL reduced or closed some of the best-hedged shorts, which can turn a hedged portfolio into a naked one. Chitra (arXiv 2512.01112) reports that Hyperliquid used ADL to close $2.1 billion of positions in 12 minutes on that day and concludes that Binance used ADL far more than Hyperliquid. Chitra's paper does not discuss hedged positions.

Correlated variants count as fewer trials than their nominal number, but new strategy families count nearly in full. The DSR paper offers N-hat = rho-hat + (1 - rho-hat) x M for M trials with average pairwise correlation rho-hat; the Notices paper suggests dimension reduction such as PCA and notes that assuming independence is conservative. In Quantt's simulation, 275 moving-average crossover variants on a zero-drift random walk had average pairwise correlation 0.65 and a best SR of 0.50, against 0.92 expected for 275 independent trials; inverting the formula gives about 10 effective independe

Authors' rule of thumb from the Notices of the AMS paper: with only 5 years of data, as few as 45 strategy configurations can produce at least one with a strong in-sample Sharpe and poor out-of-sample performance. The AMS release also says few firms or researchers actually run out-of-sample tests.

The strongest net-of-cost trend results are unreplicated backtests, not live records. AdaptiveTrend comes from a small research firm and contradicts itself on the out-of-sample window (December 2024 in Section 4.1, October 2025 in the Figure 1 caption). Zarattini et al. is a working paper in the Swiss Finance Institute series with a backtest ending 19 March 2025. In a Man Institute interview recorded in September 2022, Campbell Harvey warns that trend results can be overfit, that academic work often ignores transaction costs, and that trend lacks the capacity of some other strategies.

Most peer-reviewed crypto momentum and reversal results are gross of trading costs, and cost-adjusted out-of-sample evidence is thin. Liu, Tsyvinski and Wu say their long-short strategies ignore trading costs and short-selling feasibility, and Grobys et al. (2025) report no cost-adjusted payoffs. The cost-aware or out-of-sample results found come from one journal abstract (Fieberg et al., JFQA 2025), one rule-based study with data to 2017 (Hudson and Urquhart), and 2026 preprints, blogs and student repositories (AdaptiveTrend, the walk-forward EMA paper, the 25-coin repository, the 15-minute r

The Probability of Backtest Overfitting (PBO, Bailey, Borwein, López de Prado, Zhu) is estimated with combinatorially symmetric cross-validation (CSCV): the history is split into equal blocks and every symmetric in-sample/out-of-sample assignment is evaluated. The method is model-free and non-parametric. The authors argue that ordinary hold-out is unreliable for investment backtests.

FTI Consulting's review of the 10 October 2025 crash (more than $19B of leverage liquidated in about a day) warns that auto-deleveraging (ADL) can involuntarily close profitable shorts and turn a hedged portfolio into a naked one. Some of the best-hedged shorts were reduced or closed to protect exchange solvency. FTI advises desks that use derivatives as hedges to include ADL mechanics in counterparty due diligence. FTI does not discuss basis trades directly, so applying this to a short-perp or short-future leg of cash-and-carry is an inference.

Execution cost per dollar rises with order size, so capacity is finite even in liquid pairs. Donier and Bonart find that Bitcoin metaorder impact on MtGox Bitcoin/USD data follows a square-root law over four decades of order size, with an impact exponent near 0.5 and a Y-ratio near 0.9. On Hyperliquid, front-end traders place large aggressive orders whose size scales little with displayed liquidity and pay 2.43 bps per dollar of taker volume, against 0.70 bps for market makers who size to the book.

A Stevens Hanlon FSC / Quantm Capital student project (Bybit L2 data Oct 2023-Mar 2024, Binance OHLCV 2017-Apr 2024) found Random Forest and LSTM grid-parameter tuning did 'not offer significant improvements over traditional grid trading', while a mean-reversion hedging overlay beat simply holding BTC. The write-up does not discuss fees.

A naive market maker quoting at the touch has negative expected value after fees. Albers et al. (live Binance BTC perpetual, best fee tier) measured -0.43 bp per roundtrip net for the naive maker over 12,623 trades. Jonathan Shore, an independent practitioner with a prior HFT market-making background, computed -0.68 bp per position for a naive strategy at a 10 bp target on a year of crypto tick data (2020) and concluded that naive spread capture does not work in crypto. The two studies differ in venue and era.

A maker that keeps a constant spread through a one-directional move accumulates the losing side. In Bieganowski and Slepaczuk's 1-second Binance Futures backtest (to 2025-10-12), the simple constant-spread maker was filled repeatedly on its bid during the 2025-10-10 crash, built a growing long and took what the authors call catastrophic losses, while a taker using the same signals profited. Hummingbot's Avellaneda-Stoikov guide shows the same inventory problem for a symmetrical strategy in a BTC-USDT downtrend.

The only profitable maker variant in Albers et al. is a contrarian/balanced-inventory logistic-regression strategy at a 0.24 threshold: +0.71 bp per roundtrip (p=0.016) with minimum-size orders, holding under 10 minutes, assuming the best possible 0.5 bp maker rebate. The authors say the high Sharpe is unlikely to persist with larger orders, minor assumption changes could cut it sharply, and the profits are 'likely not scalable'.

Non-normal returns cut the number of trials a given Sharpe ratio can survive. In the DSR paper's worked example (5 years of daily data, annualized SR 2.5, N=100 trials, V[SR_n]=0.5, skewness -3, kurtosis 10) the DSR is about 0.90, below the 0.95 bar; the strategy would have passed only with N <= 46 trials, whereas with normal returns the same SR would have passed up to N=88 (recomputed here: 0.9004 at N=100, 0.9505 at N=46, N=88 for normal returns). Harvey and Liu's haircut method does not model this: they warn that a high SR from an option-like strategy with negative skew 'should be viewed in

BIS attributes the size and variation of crypto carry mainly to a volatile convenience yield, driven by trend-chasing small investors who want leveraged upside and by a shortage of arbitrage capital willing to run cash-and-carry. Interest rate differentials explain very little of the variation.

Basis series in the cited work come from Skew (BIS; CoinDesk 2020), Glassnode's 3-month annualized futures basis chart (TFTC), Coinglass for open interest and volume (Bitcoin.com News), and Bloomberg and CF Benchmarks for the CME front-month basis. The Banque de France uses CFTC Commitments of Traders data for CME positioning by investor category.

Chen, Chen and Jang (arXiv 2506.11921, submitted 2025-06-13) show that if price moves up or down by one grid step with equal probability, with no drift and no fees, a traditional grid has zero expected value. The proof ignores fees and slippage. Any grid profit in a real market therefore has to come from price dynamics such as mean reversion or drift, and costs then reduce it.

Slippage depends on asset and order size, so capacity is asset-specific. Donier and Bouchaud confirm the square-root impact law over four decades of order size on Mt. Gox Bitcoin data. In He et al.'s Kaiko sample, a 0.5 million trade in a BTC perpetual moved price by less than 0.3 bps. AdaptiveTrend's authors estimate that their small-cap short leg caps out at about 5 to 10 million dollars before slippage exceeds 10 bps per trade.

Implementations exist for the main checks. The ml4t-diagnostic library's deflated_sharpe_ratio and compute_min_trl are used in the ML4T scripts; they take raw returns, add an AR(1) variance correction, and accept a list of candidate return arrays for K>1. The R pbo package implements CSCV from a T×N return matrix, a partition count S and a performance function. A vendor export adds a per-row dsr column with the raw ingredients (srObs, skew, kurt, tradeCount) so the number can be recomputed. The expected-maximum formula is short enough to audit against Snippet 1 (getExpMaxSR) in the DSR paper.

The DSR authors have since extended the toolkit. Their 2025 ADIA Lab paper 'How to Use the Sharpe Ratio' (López de Prado, Lipton, Zoonekynd) lists five flaws in common Sharpe analysis: assuming Normal returns, ignoring significance and sample size, ignoring test power, confusing p-values with the probability an investment is effective, and not adjusting for multiple testing. It adds Bayesian false-discovery-rate methods and a hybrid single/multiple-test framework, and reports Monte Carlo results favouring them over t-tests and common corrections. Surviving strategies in that search traded only 30 to 63 times, so skew and kurtosis estimates, which DSR depends on, are noisy. DSR on small trade counts inherits that noise.

Open-source implementations of DSR and PBO exist: a pure-Python 'deflated-sharpe' package (DSR plus a Benjamini-Hochberg helper) and 'backtest-audit' (DSR, PBO, Monte Carlo permutation test, on numpy/pandas/scipy). Neither implementation was code-reviewed in this pass; check formulas against the 2014 paper before relying on them.

Two complementary multiple-testing adjustments exist for Sharpe ratios. DSR benchmarks against the extreme-value expectation of the best of N trials and needs N, trial-Sharpe variance, skew, kurtosis and T. The Harvey-Liu haircut converts the Sharpe into a t-ratio and p-value, adjusts the p-value for multiple tests with Bonferroni, Holm or BHY using an assumed number of prior tests and a user-set correlation level, and converts back into a haircut Sharpe. The DSR paper says Harvey and Liu's threshold plays an analogous role to its own and encourages computing DSR with both.

A random-forest statistical-arbitrage model on 40 coins (JRFM 2019) reported 7.1 bps of daily return after assuming 15 bps per half turn, a positive net result at much higher assumed cost than the copula study above.

Reported basis depends on the spot reference and timestamp. Standard CME bitcoin futures final-settle to BRR (4 p.m. London); BRRNY is the U.S.-close variant and IBIT's benchmark (Mallory). CME BasisWatch uses a 60-second spot TWAP from 3:59 to 4:00 p.m. ET and the nearest monthly contract, while CryptoSlate matched the 7 August settlement to the 4 p.m. ET New York benchmark. BIS takes exchange-level basis from Skew and CME positions from CFTC data, and Glassnode publishes a 3-month annualized basis chart (linked by TFTC).

Bitcoin market impact follows the square-root law over about four decades of order size (impact exponent about 0.5, Y-ratio about 0.9 with standard deviation 0.35 on MtGox data, Aug 2011 to Nov 2013), so slippage grows with the square root of order size and capacity limits are real even for liquid pairs.

A 2025 Finnish thesis hosted on Theseus, 'Bitcoin trading performance evaluation: A comparative study of momentum and mean reversion strategies from 2020 to 2025', is reported by search summaries to find mean-reverting behavior in hourly Bitcoin data, with a Bollinger-band strategy beating a moving-average momentum strategy and buy-and-hold. The thesis page returned HTTP 403, so cost treatment, parameters and any out-of-sample design are unknown.

Wen, Bouri, Xu and Zhao (North American Journal of Economics and Finance 2022; Bitcoin high-frequency data, 3 Mar 2013 to 31 May 2020) report both intraday momentum and intraday reversal in Bitcoin, with the patterns shifting around large price jumps, FOMC announcements, liquidity levels and the COVID-19 outbreak. The effect also appears in Ethereum, Litecoin and Ripple. They tie momentum to late-informed investors and the reversal, which they call unique to crypto, to overreaction and overconfidence. A timing strategy built on the predictors beats always-long and buy-and-hold in economic valu

DSR is only as honest as the trial count N. Correlated variants make the effective N much smaller than the literal count: one simulation found a 275-variant moving-average sweep behaved like about 10 independent trials (average pairwise correlation 0.65). The same source says the estimate is specific to that grid. A crypto backtest vendor states that the true number of trials behind its indicator search is probably larger than the 95.1 million it counted, so its luck bar is likely understated. An understated N makes DSR optimistic.

The luck hurdle grows only with the logarithm of the number of trials. The standardized one-term hurdle Phi^-1(1-1/N) is 3.09 sigma at N=1,000, 4.75 sigma at 1 million, 5.48 sigma at 47.5 million and 6.0 sigma at 1 billion (recomputed here; Rulyfi's table shows the same values rounded). Above about 100,000 trials each tenfold increase in search adds under half a sigma, so a genuine large edge survives deflation while a mediocre best-of-many does not. Counting trials honestly therefore costs little against real edges and a lot against flukes.

Short histories raise the best-of-N noise Sharpe. By the same formula, N=1,000 gives an expected best annualized SR of 1.88 at 3 years but 1.03 at 10 years; N=100 gives 1.46 at 3 years, 1.13 at 5 years and 0.96 at 7 years (recomputed here, i.i.d. normal null). Quantt reports the 3-year, N=1,000 figure of 1.88 and says three years is the length of many crypto and intraday backtests; that statement about typical crypto backtest length was not independently verified.

Both Bailey et al. papers give the same extreme-value approximation: for N independent zero-skill trials, E[max SR] ≈ E[SR] + √V[SR] × ((1−γ)·Z⁻¹(1−1/N) + γ·Z⁻¹(1−1/(N·e))), with γ ≈ 0.5772 (Euler-Mascheroni) and an upper bound of √(2 ln N); the DSR paper includes a Python snippet (getExpMaxSR). With a true Sharpe of zero, the annualised estimate over y years has variance about 1/y, so the best annualised Sharpe among N luck-only trials is about E[max of N standard normals] ÷ √y. The reinforcement-learning market-making papers in this evidence set show simulation or very short-sample results, not live profit. Sadighian trained on 8 days and tested on 2 days (2019-11-01 and 11-02) of Coinbase data, and several reported return entries are negative. Guo and Lin use equities, not crypto. Cekal's PPO policy lost money in both historical windows it tested, and the author says robust profitability claims 'remain out of scope'.

Dobrynskaya's study of about 2,000 coins (2014-2020) finds momentum at holding periods under one month, strongest at two-week sorting, holding and rebalancing, then reversal from about four weeks. That is far faster than the roughly one-year turn seen in equities.

Crypto return predictability changes sign with horizon and coin liquidity, so both momentum and mean reversion are observed. Reversal appears at 15-minute to 1-hour bars (Kitron and Wengrowicz; a 25-coin 30-minute test) and at the daily horizon among most coins, which are illiquid (Zaremba et al.). Momentum appears at 1-4 week lookbacks (Liu, Tsyvinski and Wu), in short formation periods that fade at longer ones in a 12-coin daily test (Tzouvanas et al.), and at daily to weekly horizons among the largest, most liquid coins (Zaremba et al.; Ficura). Controversy: Cross-sectional momentum evidence is not consistent: Grobys and Sapkota (Economics Letters 2019) report no significant momentum payoffs across 143 coins in 2014-2018 and read that as a more efficient market than earlier studies implied. Liu, Tsyvinski and Wu (Journal of Finance 2022) instead list momentum, with market and size, as one of three factors explaining cross-sectional crypto returns. The two studies differ in sample and coin universe.

Controversy: Harvey, Liu and Zhu (Review of Financial Studies 2016; NBER w20592) argue that after hundreds of tested factors the usual t-ratio > 2.0 hurdle makes no economic or statistical sense for a new factor. Their multiple-testing model puts the hurdle at t > 3.0, and they state that most claimed research findings in financial economics are likely false. Harvey and Liu (Journal of Portfolio Management 2015) cite at least 316 factors tested in the equity cross-section. Scope: the published equity literature; the papers do not cover crypto.

Controversy: How widespread false findings are in published equity factors is disputed, and the figures do not transfer to crypto.
